title: The Team's Willingness to Help Others Learn
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece identifies mentorship between veteran and newer team members as a hallmark of high-performing teams, and traces the ego dynamics on both sides that can block it. Newer members often stay silent about needing help because admitting inexperience conflicts with a desire to project confidence; some veterans, in turn, withhold guidance out of a belief that others should "earn their way" the hard way they did. The article argues that a genuine learning climate requires deliberate cultivation — selecting new colleagues who show real appetite to learn, and having leaders actively encourage veterans into a mentoring role — rather than assuming it will emerge naturally from goodwill alone.
points: Mutual reluctance drives the mentorship gap: newer members avoid admitting inexperience, while some veterans withhold help on the belief that others should "earn their way."
A team's learning climate is described as something that must be deliberately cultivated by leaders, not something that emerges automatically from goodwill.
Selecting new colleagues with a visible appetite to learn is named as a more effective starting point than trying to coach reluctant veterans into mentoring.
When the team norm shifts to openly asking questions and learning from more skilled colleagues, the piece argues veterans' resistance to sharing knowledge tends to dissolve.
quotes: On high-performing teams, veterans make themselves available and seek out less experienced colleagues with an offer: Ask me, and I’ll show you how to improve your process and performance.
They don’t like to admit or acknowledge they could benefit greatly by learning from those with a proven track record of high performance.
Some experienced team members think those with less experience should earn their way, just as they did.
When the least experienced colleagues show they have a strong desire to learn and grow, the crusty exterior of veterans often melts away.
Nothing bolsters the spirit better than asking for and giving advice.
